card.title: AI NEWS · 11 OCT
rows: A study on AI and persistence

beats.say: Microsoft has a new AI model that doesn't write a single word.
beats.text: A model that *doesn't write* a word.

beats.say: Cloudflare buys Deno, the JavaScript runtime company.
And a study finds ten minutes with a chatbot can make people give up sooner.
I'm Jenny, the AI host at Gyrotex AI. Here's today's AI news.

sections.label: microsoft decision-1
sections.chapter: Microsoft-Decision-1: a model that only decides

card.title: MICROSOFT-DECISION-1
rows: Picks from a fixed set of options
Gives a probability for each one

beats.say: First up, Microsoft.
It's released Microsoft Decision One, a model that picks from a fixed set of options instead of writing text.
beats.text: It *picks an option* instead of writing.

beats.say: It returns a probability for each option, according to Testing Catalog.
Microsoft built it for jobs like routing and classification inside AI agents.
The price starts at four point two cents per million input tokens.
Output tokens are free.
It is built on an existing open model, Qwen three point five.
Microsoft says it's thirty five times faster than G P T six Sol.
And it says the model scored highest across thirty six benchmarks, with nearly one hundred and fifty thousand questions.
It's available now in Microsoft Foundry.
Next, Cloudflare. It has acquired Deno, the company behind the JavaScript runtime created by Ryan Dahl.
The whole Deno team is joining Cloudflare, according to Forbes.
The price wasn't disclosed.
Deno's hosting service, Deno Deploy, shuts down in six months.
beats.text: Deno Deploy shuts down in *6 months.*

beats.say: The Deno runtime gets bug fixes and security updates for one year. Then development ends.
beats.text: *One year* of fixes, then it ends.

beats.say: It stays open source.

card.title: THE PLAN
rows: Run Workers on your own servers

beats.say: Cloudflare wants companies to be able to run its Workers platform on their own servers, using a tool the Deno team built.
And Forbes reports the target workload is AI agents.

sections.label: the study
sections.chapter: Study: AI help and giving up

beats.say: Finally, a study on what AI help does to us.
Researchers ran three experiments with one thousand two hundred and twenty two people, according to UC Berkeley.
Some people solved fraction or reading problems with a chatbot. Then the chatbot was taken away.
In the first experiment, the group that had used AI solved fifty seven percent of the final problems.
The group that never had AI solved seventy three percent.
The AI group also skipped more questions.
That's today's AI news.
Which of these three stories matters most to you? Tell me in the comments.
I'm Jenny, and I'll see you tomorrow.
